boundary_rationale: The opening clause of this stretch is still third-person report — צָעַ֥ק לִבָּ֖ם (oshb:Lam.2.18, byte tier), a third-person singular verb whose subject is a masculine noun carrying a third-person plural suffix — before the verse turns to imperative mood within its own line: “Their heart cried to the Lord. O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears run down like a river day and night.” web:Lam.2.18, where the second-person feminine singular imperative הוֹרִ֨ידִי (oshb:Lam.2.18, byte tier) opens a chain that continues unbroken from the second-person feminine singular address already running at the front-seam neighbor, צָרָֽיִךְ (oshb:Lam.2.17, byte tier), through “Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the watches! Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord. Lift up your hands toward him for the life of your young children, who faint for hunger at the head of every street.” web:Lam.2.19, whose four imperatives — ק֣וּמִי, רֹ֣נִּי, שִׁפְכִ֤י and שְׂאִ֧י (oshb:Lam.2.19, byte tier) — are all second-person feminine singular (a ketiv/qere note also marks this second verse per the inventory: the quoted rendering “in the night” stands on the qere word בַלַּ֗יְלָה, oshb:Lam.2.19, byte tier, not the ketiv). Whether the addressee is the wall itself or the daughter of Zion it belongs to is a question this reading holds open rather than settling; the third-person masculine-plural-suffixed heart of web:Lam.2.18 cannot itself be the addressee, since it stands as the grammatical subject of a third-person verb rather than as a form the second-person-feminine imperatives could govern.
